questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: name the setting and rhythm signals that mark a passage as verse
questions.stem: The same words are set two ways. As prose: "The lamp went out, the door swung, and the child waited in the cold until morning." As verse: the sentence is broken after "out" and after "swung." What does the second setting mark?

options.text: The breaks fall at grammatical joints, so the lines are the reader's units
The lines are shorter, so the setting is verse and the other is prose
options.misconception: treats line length as the deciding feature of verse

options.text: The punctuation is different, since verse may not use commas
options.misconception: believes verse forbids the punctuation prose uses

options.text: The words are the same, so the two settings are one passage in two forms
options.misconception: denies that setting alone can change the kind of writing

questions.explanation: Prose and verse are distinguished by the units they give a reader: prose runs in sentences inside paragraph blocks, while verse is set in lines whose breaks and rhythms are part of the meaning. Here the breaks fall where the syntax closes, so each line is a whole unit of sense and the reader's attention is organised by line rather than by sentence. The tempting arguments are about length and punctuation, but a short line is still a line of prose if it is only a break for width, and no rule forbids commas in verse.
questions.hint: Ask which unit the reader is asked to take in at a time.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: use lineation and terminal punctuation to tell verse from prose
questions.stem: A printed page reads: "The hens came up at dusk / and stood along the wire, one / after another, until the / whole fence was a line of them / and then the dark." How is this passage marked as verse?

options.text: Its line breaks fall inside the sentence and no line ends with a full stop
Its subject matter is rural, which is a standard subject for verse
options.misconception: assigns a subject matter to a formal property

options.text: It has no paragraph block, so it cannot be read as prose at all
options.misconception: believes the absence of a block settles the question on its own

options.text: Its verbs are in the present tense, which prose normally avoids
options.misconception: treats tense as a marker of verse rather than of narration

questions.explanation: Two formal signals carry the passage. The lines are set deliberately, with breaks that fall inside the sentence rather than at its ends, and no line carries terminal punctuation, so the sentence is allowed to run across the lineation. Those are the marks that make a reader process the text line by line, and they are marks about setting and punctuation, not about subject or tense. The rural reading is the classic error here, since plenty of prose is set about farms, and the present tense is a choice of narration available to prose in every period.
questions.hint: Ask whether any one line could be lifted out whole.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: compare how the same words work as prose and as verse
questions.stem: One sentence is printed as a paragraph and then as three lines, with the breaks after "long" and after "the water". What does the verse setting do to the reading that the paragraph does not?

options.text: It makes the reader pause at two named spots, holding each pause open
It shortens the text, so the verse version says less than the paragraph
options.misconception: believes setting can remove words from a sentence

options.text: It changes the tense, since lineation requires a present-tense form
options.misconception: invents a grammatical consequence of a typographic choice

options.text: It improves the rhythm, since every line in a poem should scan equally
options.misconception: treats equal line lengths as the goal of a verse setting

questions.explanation: The words and their order are identical in both settings, so anything the verse does is done by the breaks. A line ending is a point at which a reader is expected to take a breath and hold, and two deliberate breaks inside one sentence give the reader two places where the sentence hangs, which the unbroken paragraph does not. That is the whole difference, and the three tempting readings each credit the setting with something it cannot do: it removes no words, alters no tense, and imposes no requirement that lines be equal in length.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader does at the end of a line.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state where a turn conventionally falls in a quatrain-quatrain-couplet sonnet
questions.stem: A sonnet is set in three quatrains and a closing couplet, fourteen lines in all. Which line is conventionally the sonnet's turn, and what does a turn do?

options.text: The ninth line, where the argument changes direction rather than continuing
The first line, since a sonnet should announce its conclusion at the start
options.misconception: places the turn where a modern argument would place its thesis

options.text: The eleventh, since the couplet's first line is where the turn falls
options.misconception: locates the turn in the couplet and not at the octave's end

options.text: The fourteenth, since the last line is where every sonnet finally turns
options.misconception: assumes the turn is the same thing as the ending

questions.explanation: In the quatrain-quatrain-couplet sonnet the argument runs for eight lines and then turns at the ninth, which is where the octave ends, and the couplet closes it. A turn is a change of direction rather than a change of subject: the poem's problem or claim is reconsidered, and whatever follows answers the part that came before. The other placements confuse a turn with a thesis or an ending, and the third option is a plain miscount of where the octave gives way to the sestet.
questions.hint: Ask how many lines come before the argument changes direction.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: locate the volta in a given sonnet and say what changes there
questions.stem: Lines 1 to 9 of an invented sonnet: "I have argued with this gate for nine years, / and every year it holds. / I have named it, catalogued its hinges, / filed its complaints with men who do not come. / I have been owed a great deal by this gate. / I have been given a post at its foot. / I have learned the shape of the bar from the inside. / I have learned that gates are made of a kind of patience. / I have stopped arguing." What changes at line 9?

options.text: The speaker gives up the activity the first eight lines are built on
The subject changes, since the gate is replaced by the speaker's state
options.misconception: thinks a change of address is a change of subject

options.text: The tense changes, since the poem shifts tense at the ninth line
options.misconception: grounds a turn in a grammatical shift the lines do not make

options.text: The gate finally opens, which is what the argument has been preparing
options.misconception: reads the turn as the arrival of a predicted event

questions.explanation: The first eight lines are a single sustained activity: arguing, cataloguing, filing, owing, being given, learning. Line 9 withdraws from that activity by name. That is a turn in the technical sense, because the poem's relation to its subject changes rather than its subject matter, and the remaining lines can now be read as what follows the stopping. The second and third options are both true descriptions of a formal feature being mistaken for the turn, and the fourth is an invention, since nothing in the nine lines predicts an opening.
questions.hint: Ask what the first eight lines are doing that the ninth does not.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a marked turn from an unmarked one
questions.stem: Two sonnets are compared. In the first, line 9 begins "But it is only a gate." In the second, line 9 reads "It was never a gate." Both turn at the ninth line. What is the difference between the marked and the unmarked turn?

options.text: The first announces its reversal in a conjunction; the second leaves it to find
The first reverses the sense and the second only continues the argument
options.misconception: assumes a marked turn changes direction while an unmarked one does not

options.text: The first is plainer, which is what makes its turn visible to a reader
options.misconception: attributes a marked turn to register rather than to the conjunction

options.text: The first is a sestet, so its turn is conventional and the second's is not
options.misconception: confuses the location of a turn with whether it is signalled

What both sonnets share is the change of direction, which is what the first option leaves intact; the second option would make a turn a matter of announcement rather than of direction, and the fourth confuses position with signalling.
questions.hint: Ask which ninth line tells the reader it is turning.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what a stanza's shape tells a reader about the poem's units
questions.stem: A poem is set in quatrains of four lines with an alternating rhyme and a third line that argues the other side of the first two. What does that shape promise the reader?

options.text: A recurring unit in which the third line tests what the first two set up
A complete argument, since four lines is long enough to finish one
options.misconception: assumes a line count determines how much a stanza can finish

options.text: A change of speaker, since quatrains mark a change of voice by convention
options.misconception: reads a unit of lineation as a marker of who is speaking

options.text: A rhyme, since the shape's main work is the sound at the ends of lines
options.misconception: reduces a stanza's shape to its rhyme scheme

questions.explanation: A stanza's shape is a promise about recurrence: the same number of lines, the same rhyme pattern, and a structural position for the turn. In a quatrain of this kind the third line is the hinge that tests the opening, and because the shape recurs the reader knows to expect a test at the same place in every unit. The tempting readings treat the shape as a container, a speaker marker, or a sound pattern alone; a stanza is none of those by itself, and its usefulness is that it makes a position repeatable.
questions.hint: Ask what recurs at the same place in every unit.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: read a quatrain's shape as a promise about where the unit turns
questions.stem: A quatrain runs: "He mended the gate in the rain, / and the gate took it, / as gates do, / and he went without looking back." What does the shape do to the reader's expectation?

options.text: It promises a claim in the third line, and the poem declines to make it
It closes after four lines, so nothing after the fourth can revise the third
options.misconception: treats the stanza's end as a bar on any later revision

options.text: It withholds the rhyme, so the reader cannot hear the unit complete itself
options.misconception: invents a missing rhyme scheme in a quatrain that shows none

options.text: It delays the subject, since the gate is not named until it is guessed
options.misconception: misreads a subject named in the first line as one held back

questions.explanation: The quatrain's third line is where a turn usually falls, and here the turn is also a deflation: "as gates do" is a generalisation the reader expects to be the point, and the fourth line walks away instead. The shape has set the reader up for a claim at a known position, and the poem declines to make it, which is what gives the closing line its flatness. The second option mistakes a stanza boundary for a censorship, and the third and fourth invent formal problems, since the rhyme is regular and the gate is named in the first line.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: judge what a stanza's length makes possible and what it costs
questions.stem: A poem prints each stanza as a single line, wrapped by the page, and each of those lines holds a full argument with a turn in the middle. What has the shape made possible, and what has it cost?

options.text: Each argument is visibly one unit, at the price of the sense of its length
The poem is read faster, since shorter visual units always move a reader on
options.misconception: believes shorter units always increase reading speed

options.text: The arguments are more important, since a line each values them by form
options.misconception: infers a hierarchy of importance from a formal assignment

options.text: The poem is more modern, since long stanzas are a recent invention
options.misconception: dates a formal choice as recent when the form is centuries old

questions.explanation: One argument to one line makes the unit unambiguous: whatever the wrapped line contains is the whole of that unit, and a reader can see where it begins. The cost is metrical and spatial, because a line that runs to the edge of the measure gives the eye no regular place to rest, so a reader loses the sense of a stanza's duration. The three tempting readings turn a visual arrangement into an effect it cannot have: shorter units are not automatically faster, a form's choices say nothing about the importance of their contents, and long single-line stanzas are not a modern invention.

questions.learningObjective: identify the marks of a deliberate break with narrative order
questions.stem: A novel opens on a woman running for a train, gives her the name Margit only on page 40, and explains the reason for the run fifty pages after the running. What marks this as a break with order?

options.text: The naming and the explanation both arrive after what they account for
The chapter order is wrong, since a novel should move forward through time
options.misconception: assumes any unusual order is a misplacement of chapters

options.text: The point of view changes, since two people are called Margit
options.misconception: invents a second person to explain a change in narration

options.text: The prose is modern, since a book like this cannot be eighteenth-century
options.misconception: dates a formal choice rather than identifying the feature in it

questions.explanation: A break with narrative order shows up as information delivered out of sequence: a reader meets an effect before its cause, or a name after the person has been moving through the book as someone else. Here both the name and the reason are late, so the early pages ask a reader to hold an unexplained action, and the later pages supply what the earlier ones withheld. The other three options each attribute the effect to something the description does not contain: no chapter is misplaced, only one person is called Margit, and a formal choice says nothing about a book's date.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: describe the order a disrupted narrative uses
questions.stem: A chapter runs: "The door was open. Someone had been in the room. I put my bag down and waited for her, and she did not come, and I understood that she was not coming." Only then does it begin: "It was a Tuesday, and I had walked from the station." What order is the chapter using?

options.text: Consequence before circumstance, so the reader receives the effect first
A flashback, since the later paragraph is a memory of the earlier one
options.misconception: names the device from the fact of lateness rather than from the effect

options.text: A frame story, since the first paragraph introduces a separate narrative
options.misconception: treats a single chronology as though two stories were being told

options.text: An unreliable narrator, since the two paragraphs disagree about the time
options.misconception: concludes a fault in the narrator from an order the chapter declares

questions.explanation: The chapter withholds its circumstances and gives its consequences first: a door, an intruder, a wait, an ending, and only then a day and a walk to explain any of it. That is a deliberate inversion of exposition, and its point is that a reader who arrives at the explanation has already lived through the waiting. The second option names a device from the bare fact of lateness, which every retelling has; the third invents a second story in a single chronology; and the fourth mistakes a declared order for a contradiction, which would need a claim the chapter never makes.
questions.hint: Ask which paragraph a reader would write first in telling a friend.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a deliberate break in order from merely difficult writing
questions.stem: A chapter gives a character two names, three contradictory seasons for one week, and no signal that any of this is being done on purpose. Which reading is best supported?

options.text: None yet, since a break reads as deliberate only when a text invites it
A deliberate break, since breaking order is a recognised modern technique
options.misconception: names a movement as a technique and treats the naming as evidence

options.text: A deliberate break, since the contradictions are too regular to be accidental
options.misconception: infers design from a pattern without asking whether the text marks it

options.text: Merely bad writing, since an unmarked break can only be carelessness
options.misconception: divides the possibilities into designed and careless and allows no middle

questions.explanation: A break in narrative order is not the same as an error, and a reader cannot tell which one they are looking at from strangeness alone. What makes a break legible as designed is some signal the text offers: a recurrence that returns on a schedule, an epigraph, a formal rule the book states, a pattern the reader can hold. Without one, the description gives a reader reasons to suspect a muddle, and the three tempting options each take a shortcut, naming a technique, inferring design from neatness, or assuming that any unmarked irregularity must be a mistake.
questions.hint: Ask what the text gives a reader to hold on to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a realist claim from a romantic one
questions.stem: One novel's opening gives a table of wages, a floor plan of the worker's lodging, and the names of the two families who share a well. Another gives a boy's vision of the moon, his certainty that it has been waiting for him, and the sound it makes. Which opening is making which claim?

options.text: The first claims ordinary causes, the second claims an inner experience
The first is romantic, since a table of wages is a form of poetry
options.misconception: suggests a form of expression rather than a kind of claim

options.text: Both are realist, since neither admits anything it cannot account for
options.misconception: treats the plainness of one and the marvel of the other as equally testable

options.text: The order cannot be decided, since a real book can use wages and a moon
options.misconception: refuses to weigh the claims because the two devices are compatible

questions.explanation: The difference between the movements is a difference in what a text claims about the world, not in its props. The realist claim is that ordinary conditions and ordinary causes account for what happens, so wages, a floor plan, and a shared well are offered as the mechanism of a life. The romantic claim treats the exceptional moment and the inward feeling as the real thing, so a moon that has been waiting is not a detail but a claim. A real book can hold both, which is why the fourth option's compatibility argument settles nothing; the claims have to be weighed separately.
questions.hint: Ask in each case whether the extraordinary is being explained or asserted.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: classify two passages by the kind of claim they make
questions.stem: Passage A: "The rent was due on the fifth, the wages came on the sixth, and so the family was always one week short, which is arithmetic and not misfortune." Passage B: "The rent was due on the fifth, and something in him rose to meet it, as though the fact of a debt were a kind of weather." Which passage makes the romantic claim?

options.text: B, because it turns an external fact into a claim about what he felt
A, because its flat tone is what a realist claim sounds like
options.misconception: judges a passage's movement by its tone rather than by its claim

options.text: Neither, because both begin with the same detail of a rent falling due
options.misconception: treats a shared detail as evidence that the two claims agree

options.text: A, because it names the cause of the shortfall and B does not
options.misconception: finds the movement in whether a cause is supplied

questions.explanation: Passage B makes the romantic claim because it substitutes an interior response for a cause: a debt falling due becomes "weather" felt "in him," which is a claim that the moment's meaning lies in the feeling rather than in the facts. Passage A is the realist claim at work, since the sentence names wages, dates, and an arithmetic shortfall and then insists that the arithmetic is the whole of it. The two tempting readings that pick A are both reasonable-sounding and both wrong for the same reason: they judge by tone, or by whether a cause is stated, instead of by what is being claimed.
questions.hint: Ask which passage says what the fact caused, and which says what it meant.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a realist passage gains by refusing the exceptional
questions.stem: A realist novel narrates a man's whole week in full, including the parts where nothing improves. What does the chapter gain by refusing an exceptional moment?

options.text: The reader is held inside the ordinary, so no crisis explains anything
The week is proved important, since only a serious matter deserves detail
options.misconception: measures a passage's value by the size of the event it records

options.text: The chapter is made more readable, since predictable events are easier to follow
options.misconception: credits a narrative's realism with a technical ease in reading

options.text: The man's character is made good, since he endures what cannot be changed
options.misconception: reads endurance as a moral verdict from the fact of recording it

questions.explanation: A realist chapter's method is to refuse the moment that would let a reader feel a change without a reason. By narrating the whole week, the chapter keeps the reader at the level of ordinary conditions, and that is what removes the available explanations: nothing dramatic happens, so nothing has to be said to account for it. The three tempting readings all read the detail as doing something it cannot do, since recording a week at length does not prove its importance, does not make reading easier, and does not pass a moral judgment on the man who lives it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is not allowed to reach for.

questions.learningObjective: state what a satire attacks and by what means
questions.stem: A satire describes a committee's minute-taking in the register of epic battle: the pens are advanced, the amendments deployed, and one clause is said to have been "defeated in open session." What is the satire doing?

options.text: Applying a serious form to a small subject, so the disproportion is the joke
Describing the committee accurately, since committees use such words
options.misconception: reads a mock-heroic register as a report of institutional idiom

options.text: Praising the committee, since only great bodies earn grand treatment
options.misconception: takes the elevated register as praise rather than as the means of attack

options.text: Warning the reader about procedure, so the minute can be followed
options.misconception: assumes the purpose of a satirical passage is instruction

The second and third take the elevated language at face value, as report or as praise, which is precisely the reading a satire is built to prevent, and the fourth mistakes the passage's aim, since nobody needs a procedure to follow a satire's battle.

questions.learningObjective: state the function a gothic convention serves
questions.stem: A gothic novel opens with a castle whose owner is away, a servant who will not go past a certain corridor, and weather that arrives whenever anyone leaves the grounds. What do these conventions do?

The test has two halves and both have to be satisfied: a claim has to be arguable, which means a careful reader could decide against it, and it has to be reachable, which means the evidence an essay would gather can actually cover the extent of the claim. Student A's statement fails the first half in the most direct way available, because a question about a poem's form is settled by counting lines and reading the shape, and there is nothing left for an essay to dispute.
